title: Meta CEO Adam Mosseri Warns AI Negativity Will Intensify, Sparks Industry Alarm
body:
Instagram’s head of product, Adam Mosseri, warned that the public’s growing frustration with artificial intelligence is unlikely to subside—in fact, he expects it to intensify across a broad range of sectors, not just the creative industries that have dominated recent headlines. Speaking to a media outlet about the platform’s evolving relationship with AI, Mosseri argued that the underlying anxiety stems from a deeper fear of being left behind as generative tools reshape work, culture and personal expression.

Mosseri’s comments come at a moment when AI‑driven technologies are moving from niche research labs into everyday consumer products. From text‑to‑image generators that can produce photorealistic artwork in seconds to large language models that draft emails, code and news stories, the speed of adoption has outpaced public understanding. While many users celebrate the convenience and creative possibilities, a growing contingent voices concerns about authenticity, job displacement and the erosion of human skill. “The negativity is not a passing phase,” Mosseri said. “It’s a symptom of people feeling threatened by a technology they don’t fully grasp, and that feeling will only deepen as AI becomes more capable.”

The Instagram chief highlighted that the backlash is not limited to artists, musicians or designers—professions traditionally seen as vulnerable to automation. “We’re hearing pushback from educators, journalists, even small‑business owners who wonder whether AI will make their expertise obsolete,” he explained. This broader unease reflects a shift in the narrative: AI is no longer a curiosity for the avant‑garde; it is becoming a core component of tools that millions rely on daily. As platforms like Instagram integrate AI features for content recommendation, automated moderation and even caption generation, users are confronted with algorithmic decisions that affect visibility and revenue, fueling suspicion about fairness and control.

Industry analysts echo Mosseri’s assessment, noting that the “AI fatigue” phenomenon could have tangible consequences for tech companies. A recent survey by the Pew Research Center found that 57 % of Americans feel uneasy about AI’s influence on society, and that number rises sharply among those who work in fields where automation is already making inroads. If negative sentiment translates into reduced engagement or regulatory pressure, platforms may need to rethink how they roll out new AI capabilities. Transparency, clearer user controls and robust accountability mechanisms are being touted as essential steps to mitigate backlash.

For Instagram, the challenge is twofold. On one hand, AI can enhance user experience—improving discoverability, reducing spam, and offering creative tools that democratize content creation. On the other, the same technology can amplify concerns about deepfakes, misinformation and the dilution of authentic human expression. Mosseri suggested that the company is focusing on “human‑in‑the‑loop” approaches, where AI assists rather than replaces the creator, and on educating users about how the algorithms work. Such strategies aim to rebuild trust, but they require sustained investment and clear communication.

Looking ahead, the trajectory Mosseri describes points to a prolonged period of negotiation between technological advancement and societal acceptance. As AI models become more sophisticated and their outputs harder to distinguish from human‑made work, the conversation is likely to shift from novelty to ethics, governance and the very definition of creativity. Companies that can balance innovation with responsible stewardship may find a competitive edge, while those that ignore the mounting unease risk alienating users and attracting stricter oversight. The coming years will test whether the tech industry can transform current negativity into a constructive dialogue that shapes AI’s role in everyday life.
